problems.stem: A teacher annotates a transcript by highlighting two turns in yellow and writing 'good thinking here.' What is the core methodological weakness?
options: Yellow is hard to read on screen.
There is no defined code scheme, so another rater could not reproduce which turns count as reasoning.
The note is too short to earn full marks.
The teacher highlighted two turns instead of one.
problems.explanation: Annotation is a method; without a reproducible code scheme the judgment is just subjective highlighting.

problems.stem: A turn is coded RE (reasoning). What must accompany that code to make the annotation defensible?
options: The time the turn was spoken.
A warrant naming the specific phrase or move in the turn that justifies the reasoning label.
A count of how many words the student used.
problems.explanation: A code without a warrant cannot be inspected; the warrant ties the label to evidence in the turn.

problems.stem: Before reporting an annotation as evidence, which check tells you the code scheme is sound rather than personal?
options: Whether a colleague applying the same code definitions would code the same turns the same way.
Whether the transcript is at least ten turns long.
Whether the AI generated the transcript quickly.
problems.explanation: Inter-rater agreement is the test of a reproducible annotation method.

problems.stem: Using the CL/QU/RE scheme, a student says 'If the teacher allowed it, it is not cheating, so the rule depends on the assignment.' Which coding and warrant is most defensible?
options: CL, because the student stated an opinion.
RE, with the warrant that the student now conditions cheating on teacher permission, revising the earlier categorical claim.
QU, because the sentence contains the word if.
No code, because the turn is too long to classify.
problems.explanation: The turn revises the prior fixed claim by adding a condition, which is reasoning (RE) with a clear warrant.
